definition: Round-trip translation (RTT), also known as back-and-forth translation, recursive translation and bi-directional translation, is the process of translating a word, phrase or text into another language (forward translation), then translating the result back into the original language (back translation), using machine translation (MT) software.
details: It is often used by laypeople to evaluate a machine translation system, or to test whether a text is suitable for MT when they are unfamiliar with the target language. Because the resulting text can often differ substantially from the original, RTT can also be a source of entertainment.

explainer.lead: Round-trip translation translates text into another language and then back into the original, using machine translation. Laypeople often use it to gauge an MT system or check whether text suits translation.

tiers.eli5: You say something in English, translate it to French, then translate the French back to English to see how much survived the trip.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it as a rough sanity check and sometimes as a paraphrasing or data-augmentation trick. A pitfall is treating round-trip fidelity as a quality measure: the returned text can differ substantially from the original, so it is not a reliable evaluation.
tiers.paperLevel: The process is forward translation then back translation via MT software; there is no formal guarantee that the round trip preserves meaning, and divergences are common, so it is informally used rather than as a validated metric.

explainer.example: Translating 'The bank is closed' to French and back may return 'The shore is closed', revealing an ambiguity the forward translation resolved wrongly.
